newsitem.title: INDIA: INDIA CONGRESS STRESSES LOCAL CAPITAL OVER FOREIGN.
newsitem.headline: INDIA CONGRESS STRESSES LOCAL CAPITAL OVER FOREIGN.

text.p: India's Congress party on Friday pledged its commitment to economic reforms, but said foreign investment was welcome only on the nation's terms.
"Whenever capital comes from abroad it will come on our terms and conditions," former finance minister Manmohan Singh said, moving the party's economic resolution at its plenary session.
"It is the sovereign decision of the people of India to decide where foreign capital should go."

Singh said there should be greater reliance on domestic capital. "The role of foreign capital is small relative to domestic capital. India must step up its savings rate to mobilise its domestic funds," he added.
Singh, a free-market radical, launched liberalisation policies under former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao by opening up trade and industry and dismantling decades old socialist control.
The Congress party reaffirmed its faith in economic reforms but said the liberalisation policies must alleviate poverty.
It said the performance of the economy had slipped under Prime Minister Inder Kumar's Gujral's government.

"In the last one year, when Congress has been out of power, (economic) growth has declined, industrial growth fell from 12 percent to 7.0 percent, and exports dropped from 20 percent to 4.0 percent," Singh said.
India's exports rose by 4.01 percent in 1996/97 (April/March) to $33.11 billion compared with $31.83 billion in the previous year.
The Commerce Ministry said last week that exports fell by 0.95 percent to $8.13 billion in the first quarter of 1997/98.
India's industrial growth in 1996/97 (April/March) slumped to 6.7 percent from 11.6 percent the previous year.

"Due to sluggishness of industrial production and imports, the fiscal outlook is highly uncertain," the economic resolution said. "The mounting oil pool deficit constitutes a serious threat to fiscal stability."
The oil pool deficit, the money owed by the government to the oil companies to subsidise petroleum products, is currently estimated at about 190 billion rupees ($5.32 billion).
India hopes to reduce its fiscal deficit as percentage of gross domestic product (GDP) to 4.5 percent in 1997/98 (April-March) from 5.0 percent in the previous year.
"Exports seem to have lost the dynamism they acquired during the Congress rule," the resolution said.
Congress blamed a weak United Front government for the poor performance of the economy.
"The authority of the central government to maintain social and economic discipline in this vast polity of ours has considerably weakened," the resolution added.
The nation's creaking infrastructure, mainly in power, telecommunications and petroleum, needed to be revived to achieve a higher rate of economic growth, it said.
"We cannot develop the economy and remove poverty unless we improve infrastructure," Singh said. "Congress was committed to a vibrant and strong public sector," Singh said.
"Those public sector units which are profitable should be freed from bureaucratic hurdles," he added.
Singh criticised the main opposition and the left-wing parties for charging the Congress with deserting the ideology of "Swadeshi (economic nationalism)".
"Congress's commitment to strengthening and building a self-reliant national economy is as strong as ever," Singh said.
